projects.title: Personalization: On-Device Image Learning
projects.summary: iOS app that learns new image classes from a handful of photos entirely on the phone: a frozen Core ML backbone turns each photo into a vector, a small classifier is fit on the device, and only the vectors are stored.

images.alt: Personalization architecture diagram: offline experiments on a laptop and the on-device pipeline on iPhone
Teach screen of the Personalization iOS app (simulator)
Library screen of the Personalization iOS app with sample classes (simulator)

metrics.label: DINOv2-small, 1 photo per class, 5-way (nearest class mean)
Classes still recognized after learning 10 in sequence, MobileNetV3 (nearest class mean vs logistic head without replay)
Real iPhone vs Python embeddings, MobileNetV3, 20 images
metrics.source: personalization README, gate check (Debug build, one device)

projects.details: A Swift package (PersonalizeCore) holds the embedding store and two classifier heads and is checked against a Python reference; a SwiftUI app handles teaching, recognizing and a library of classes; Python scripts run the experiments and convert PyTorch backbones to Core ML.

caseStudy.role: Author of the repository: built the Swift package, the SwiftUI app, the Python experiments and the Core ML conversion.
caseStudy.problem: Teaching an app your own objects usually means uploading photos to a server. This app learns new classes from a few photos on the phone itself, with no network code, so nothing leaves the device.

decisions.choice: Freeze a Core ML backbone and fit only a small classifier head on the device
decisions.tradeoff: Learning from one or two photos is fast and cheap, but accuracy depends on the backbone: MobileNetV3 at one photo per class is the weakest result (0.834) versus 0.996 for DINOv2-small.

decisions.choice: Store only embedding vectors, not photos, and ship no network code or analytics
decisions.tradeoff: Privacy rests on build settings and a source audit, not a formal guarantee, and photos are kept if the user turns off deleting them after embedding.

decisions.choice: Offer two heads: nearest class mean and a logistic head
decisions.tradeoff: Nearest class mean never forgets earlier classes because class means don't change; logistic is slightly better for MobileNetV3 at five photos (+0.009) but forgets almost everything without replay.

decisions.choice: Check the Swift classifier against the Python reference with a shared fixture
decisions.tradeoff: Probabilities agree within 1e-4, but that only proves the Swift code matches my own Python code, not that either is optimal.

caseStudy.result: On a 2000-image Flowers102 subset, DINOv2-small reaches 0.996 accuracy with one photo per class (5-way) and rejects unseen classes with AUROC 0.994. On one real iPhone, MobileNetV3 embeddings matched the Python ones with mean cosine 0.9945. Not yet measured: on-device latency, the Pets dataset, photos from real users, and a phone check for the DINO models. The numbers are a preview.

projects.summary: Binary brain-tumor classification (ResNet) and pixel-level segmentation (U-Net) on MRI scans, with a Streamlit viewer.

metrics.label: Classifier accuracy on 747 held-out MRI scans (was 74.0% before the fixes)
Classifier ROC AUC (was 0.799); tumor recall 98.6%, healthy recall 95.5%

projects.details: Situation: Early detection of tumors in radiology scans was inconsistent. Problem: High false negatives in automated diagnosis. Action: Trained U-Net for segmentation and ResNet for classification. Result: 97.1% accuracy and 0.989 ROC AUC on 747 held-out scans (leak-free split), and 0.734 Dice for segmentation on unseen patients.

caseStudy.role: Author of the repository: designed and built it.
caseStudy.problem: Flag whether an MRI scan shows a tumor and, if so, localize it at pixel level.

decisions.choice: Two separate models: a ResNet classifier and a U-Net segmenter
decisions.tradeoff: Each is simple to train and evaluate (accuracy, F1, ROC AUC; Dice, IoU), but they are not a single joint model.

decisions.choice: Binary classification on single-modality scans first
decisions.tradeoff: Simpler problem; multi-class (glioma, meningioma, pituitary) and multi-modal input are future work.

decisions.choice: Ship a Streamlit app to visualize predictions
decisions.tradeoff: Easy to inspect outputs, though it is a demo, not a clinical tool.

caseStudy.result: Classifier: on 747 held-out scans it reaches 97.1% accuracy and 0.989 ROC AUC, up from 74.0% and 0.799. It catches 360 of 365 tumors and falsely flags 17 of 382 healthy scans. The biggest gain came from fixing input preprocessing (the ImageNet ResNet50 was fed [0,1] images instead of the 0-255 caffe-style input it expects). The split is now grouped by perceptual hash because about 2,100 of the 4,600 images are copies of the same scan, so the old 74% was probably flattering. Grad-CAM shows the evidence for 'tumor' falling on the lesion. Segmentation: the U-Net scores Dice 0.734 (IoU 0.579) on 330 slices from 11 patients it never saw. It is weaker per slice: mean Dice 0.559 on slices that contain tumor, tumors found in 69.7% of those slices, and 10.4% of tumor-free slices get a false mask. Most misses are small tumors at the edge of the volume. Web-sourced slices from mixed scanners: this is a research project, not a clinical tool.

projects.title: ModelGuard: ML Reliability Platform
projects.summary: Python library and Streamlit dashboard that detects data drift, missing features and falling accuracy in deployed models, with a drift simulator to measure how fast and reliably it notices.

images.alt: KS and PSI on the drifted feature with alerts
ModelGuard: ML Reliability Platform architecture diagram
ModelGuard dashboard: scenario summary, detection delay and alert feed
Missing-value heatmap per feature
Rolling accuracy and F1 against alert floors

metrics.label: Scenarios detected (4 drift scenarios, 3 detector settings)

projects.details: Monitor machine learning models for data drift, missing features, and declining performance. ModelGuard lets users simulate production failures, compare detection methods, and evaluate monitoring systems through reproducible experiments.

caseStudy.role: Author of the repository: designed and built it.
caseStudy.problem: A deployed model rarely fails loudly: input data shifts, a feature goes missing, and accuracy erodes weeks before labels arrive to prove it. ModelGuard watches for those three failures and alerts only when they persist.

decisions.choice: Alert only after 3 consecutive breaching batches
decisions.tradeoff: One noisy batch never pages anyone, but detection can't be faster than three batches.

decisions.choice: All state in one SQLite file; the dashboard is read-only and never calls the monitors
decisions.tradeoff: Simple and reproducible, but single-process and not load-tested.

decisions.choice: Tune thresholds on seeds 0–9 under a false-alarm budget, report on seeds 10–29
decisions.tradeoff: A held-out seed split, not a held-out data split; drift is synthetic, injected into one public dataset with one fixed model.

caseStudy.result: On synthetic drift injected into the Adult dataset, every scenario was detected in 20/20 held-out runs for every detector setting, with mean detection delay between 1.55 and 4.50 batches and one false alarm across 800 clean batches. These are synthetic-drift results, not evidence about real production traffic.

images.alt: infserve: Dynamic-Batching Inference Server architecture diagram

projects.title: infserve: Dynamic-Batching Inference Server
projects.summary: FastAPI inference server with an asyncio dynamic batcher on ONNX Runtime, plus benchmarks of what batching buys under load.
projects.details: Design stage: the repository currently holds the architecture and plan. Planned: a bounded queue that returns 429 when full, a batcher that flushes on max batch size or max wait, ONNX Runtime workers in fp32 and int8, an open-loop load generator, and p50/p95/p99 latency, queue depth and throughput metrics. Benchmarks will compare batching off vs on and fp32 vs int8. No numbers are reported yet.

images.alt: tsbench: Anomaly-Detection Benchmark architecture diagram

projects.title: tsbench: Anomaly-Detection Benchmark
projects.summary: Benchmark showing how much the ranking of time-series anomaly detectors depends on the evaluation metric, including point-adjusted scoring.
projects.details: Design stage: the repository currently holds the architecture and plan. Planned: z-score, STL residual, Isolation Forest, LOF, ARIMA, matrix profile and autoencoder detectors plus random and flag-all baselines on NAB and UCR, scored with point-wise, point-adjusted, event-based, AUC and detection-delay metrics over 5 seeds with bootstrap intervals and Wilcoxon tests. No results are reported yet.

experiences.summary: Built an unsupervised clustering pipeline that groups post-manufacturing chip failures by underlying root cause, running in production.
built: Built an unsupervised pipeline using HDBSCAN with Manhattan distance to group failures that share a root cause, with no labeled ground truth.
Engineered statistical features that capture a failure's real signature rather than surface similarity, alongside anomaly detection workflows.
Worked with domain engineers who reviewed the clusters and confirmed or rejected groupings, building ground truth iteratively.
Architected Snowflake and GCP/Azure workflows over large-scale failure analysis data, delivering cluster output to engineers as Jira tickets.
experiences.context: Summer internship on a failure analysis team in semiconductor manufacturing. Failures that look alike often have different root causes, and failures that look different can share one, so I grouped them by root cause so engineers can fix a cluster once instead of investigating every chip. Employer work, so details are kept high level.
impact: Pipeline runs in production: Snowflake data, GCP clustering, output as Jira tickets.
Engineers work on grouped failure modes instead of every individual chip.

experiences.summary: Built three internal tools for a steel manufacturer's IT & Digitalization team: a plate-mill finished-goods date forecaster, a stockyard allocation optimizer, and a blast furnace data system.
built: Plate Mill FG Date Forecasting: after interviewing users and cleaning historical data, engineered features with Gini index and SHAP values and compared ARIMA, Random Forest, Prophet and XGBoost. XGBoost performed best and was used to predict finished-goods creation dates to support dispatch planning and on-time, in-full (OTIF) delivery.

Last Point Distribution Analysis: grouped customers and stockyards with KNN clustering and geospatial analysis, then used OSRM distance APIs and historical costs to estimate transport cost, in a Streamlit app, to optimize how finished goods are allocated to stockyards.

Blast Furnace Lab system: built a centralized data management system with Spring Boot (Java) and Angular on Microsoft SQL Server, secured it with JWT authentication, and deployed it to a remote server on Tomcat for company-wide access.
experiences.context: Two-month summer internship in the Digitalization team of the IT & Communications department at Jindal Steel & Power, working with plate mill, logistics and blast furnace stakeholders.
impact: The forecasting model supports dispatch planning and on-time, in-full delivery for the plate mill.

The blast furnace system centralized lab data collection with secure, company-wide access for performance analysis.
